title: Shopping
goal: Go shopping: ask prices, name colors and sizes, and pay.
bekal: ask and understand prices with *Cé mhéad …?*
name colors, and know that colors change after feminine nouns
use standard shop phrases: trying on, asking for another size, paying

notes: **Tá geansaí uaim — "a sweater is from me".** To say "I need" or "I want", Irish uses the preposition *ó* ("from") with its pronoun forms: *uaim, uait, uaidh, uaithi, uainn, uaibh, uathu*. Literally "something is wanted **from** me". This is the fourth preposition that swallows its pronoun, after *ag*, *ar*, and *le*.

**Ceann gorm — ceann means "one" for things.** The word *ceann* (originally "head") is used just like English "one": *ceann gorm* ("a blue one"), *ceann mór* ("a big one"), *ceann eile* ("another one"), *an ceann seo* ("this one"). It stands in for a noun that is already clear from the conversation.

**Níos mó — how to compare.** *Níos* + the comparative form: *níos mó* (bigger), *níos lú* (smaller), *níos fearr* (better), *níos measa* (worse), *níos daoire* (more expensive), *níos saoire* (cheaper). To say what you're comparing with, use *ná*: *níos mó ná é seo* ("bigger than this one").

**Bain triail as — commands with a preposition at the end.** Many Irish expressions keep a prepositional pronoun at the end: *Bain triail as* ("try it"), *Suigh síos* ("sit down"), *Tar isteach* ("come in"), *Éist liom* ("listen to me"). Phrases like these are best learned whole.

blocks.text: Irish has **two** words for green, and the choice is about origin, not shade. *Glas* is for green that grows — grass, leaves, the sea. *Uaine* is for man-made green — paint, fabric, traffic lights. Swapping them doesn't make a sentence wrong, but it instantly sounds bookish.

blocks.title: Colors change after feminine nouns
items: An adjective attached to a feminine noun gets séimhiú: *léine bhán* (a white shirt; *léine* is feminine), *scairf chorcra*, *grian bhuí*.
After masculine nouns there's no change: *cóta dearg*, *geansaí gorm*, *hata donn*.
After plural nouns, the adjective adds *-a* or turns slender: *bróga dubha*, *tithe bána*, *fir mhóra*.
When the adjective comes after *tá*, it never changes: *Tá an léine bán*, *Tá na bróga dubh*. The change only happens when it is attached directly to its noun.

blocks.text: The most common comparatives: *níos mó* (bigger), *níos lú* (smaller), *níos daoire* (more expensive), *níos saoire* (cheaper), *níos fearr* (better), *níos measa* (worse). Note that *níos fearr* and *níos measa* look nothing like their base words *maith* and *olc* — just like English "good / better" and "bad / worse".
